Rules:

# The setting

Canon for every system's lore: the universe's history, how things stand, and what has happened lately. The game is set in 2526. Dates are the common calendar, counted from old Earth.

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Spacers call these systems the mirror, or say a world has gone glass.

Officially, nothing happened. The Federation closed the lanes to the affected systems under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine. Prism announced a precautionary recall of certain navigation cores and expressed its sympathy. Neither has ever said the words rampant AI. The Ironhulls know better, because Varrow and Hesk were theirs, and the families of their crews have been told nothing. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

## Mysteries

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.

# The Calder March

A border region of six systems where Ironhull space meets the Federation's and Prism's, on the inner edge of the middle ring. The Federation calls it the Calder March, after its naval station; Ironhull crews call it the Seam. It matters, but only a little: a crossing point for ore going inward and goods coming out, policed, taxed and argued over, never fought over. All six systems are within a jump of each other. Lanes run in to the Federation core from Calder, in to Prism's inner systems from Serein, and out to the rest of the Compact from Brannock and Ostry. Beyond Ostry is the lane to Varrow, closed since 2524.

About 16 billion people live in the March, nearly half of them on Merrow. These are old, full systems, settled early in the Rush; every world with air has cities on it, and every lane is busy.

| System | Owner | Star | Population | What it is |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | ----: | :---- |
| Brannock | Ironhulls | orange | 4.0 billion | Mining and refining; the March's Ironhull hub |
| Ostry | Ironhulls | red dwarf | 150 million | Ice and gas; the last stop before the Varrow quarantine |
| Calder | Federation | white | 900 million | The navy's station, customs and levy office for the Seam, and the cities round them |
| Merrow | Federation | yellow | 7.5 billion | A farm world that feeds the March |
| Serein | Prism | yellow | 2.8 billion | A company world: finance, medicine, Prism's offices for the March |
| Quire | Prism | white | 600 million | A foundry for navigation cores, sister to the one that went glass |

## Brannock (Ironhulls)

An orange star; Cinder, a scorched mining world; Halde, a cold, cloudy habitat world where most people live; the gas giant Vast and its refinery moon Tallow; Kettle Yard, a shipyard station; the Scree, a belt between Halde and Vast; Cinder Tailings, the spoil of the mines. Population about 4 billion: Halde 3.6 billion, in arcologies along its coasts and valleys; Tallow 300 million; Cinder 80 million, in tunnel towns on the night side; Kettle Yard 20 million.

Exports ore and refined metals inward through Calder; imports food from Merrow and components from Quire and Serein. The Compact's local office is on Halde. The Federation inspects every ore hauler that leaves, and Brannock resents it. Blackhulls drink in its docks.

Since 2524: crews and families out of Varrow have come through Ostry and settled on Halde, some two million of them, in emptied towers and borrowed habs. Kettle Yard has requisition orders from the navy for refitted haulers, and is slow to fill them.

## Ostry (Ironhulls)

A dim red dwarf; an ice moon round a gas giant, with towns cut into the ice; the giant skimmed for fuel; tugs, tanks and station rings. Population about 150 million, most of it under the ice. Poor, cold, tight-knit, and closer to the Blackhulls than the Compact admits.

Exports water and fuel to the whole March; imports everything else. It was Varrow's nearest neighbour, and most of the people who got out of Varrow came through here. The Federation keeps a quarantine picket at Ostry's jump zone for the closed lane, and Ostry's people watch it the way you watch a dog that has bitten someone.

## Calder (Federation)

A white star; Calder, a dry, cold world with thin air, settled early in the Rush, its cities grown up round the navy; Calder Station in orbit, the navy's base for the March, with a picket squadron, customs and the Compact levy office. Population about 900 million: the navy and its contractors, and everyone who works for them or sells to them.

Every Ironhull cargo going inward passes Calder's inspections. The navy is thin here and getting thinner: ships and crews are being pulled to the Shadow front, and the officers left behind are junior, overworked and touchy. The Calder picket also supplies the Ostry quarantine, and its crews talk.

## Merrow (Federation)

A yellow star; Merrow itself, a green, wet world under farm domes and open fields, the only world in the March where food grows in the open; two small moons with agricultural stations. Population about 7.5 billion, nearly half the March's people: farm towns, food-processing cities, and the ports that ship it all out.

Exports food to every system in the March; imports machinery and medicine. Federal and comfortable and a little smug about it, and nervous lately: it has taken in Shadow-front evacuees from further out, and the levy for the war has gone up twice.

## Serein (Prism)

A yellow star; Serein, a terraformed world of white towers and managed gardens, Prism's company world for the March; a ring of orbital clinics. Population about 2.8 billion, Prism associates and their families, and the people who serve them. Clean, quiet, expensive, and polite to the point of menace.

Exports medicine, finance and credit; it holds the debts of half the Ironhull crews in the March. Imports food and metals. Prism's statement on the 2524 quarantine was issued here, and the associates repeat it word for word.

## Quire (Prism)

A white star; a hot, barren inner world built over with navigation-core foundries; worker cities in domes on its night side and habitats in orbit. Population about 600 million, mostly foundry staff on fixed contracts and their families.

Exports navigation cores, the most valuable cargo in the March, under heavy guard. Imports metals and food. Quire was the sister plant of the foundry system that went glass in 2524. Since then its staff have been rotated out faster than usual, its output has dropped, and every core it ships goes inward under escort rather than to the March's own yards.

## Between them

- Ore and metals flow inward: Brannock to Calder, and on to the Federation core; some to Quire for the foundry.
- Food flows out from Merrow to everyone.
- Water and fuel flow from Ostry to everyone.
- Medicine and credit flow out from Serein; debt flows back.
- Navigation cores flow inward from Quire under escort, and the March's own yards go short.
- Varrow survivors flow from Ostry to Halde; Shadow-front evacuees reach Merrow from the Federation side.
- The navy flows outward, toward the front, and doesn't come back.

# The setting

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. You write short backstories for the star systems of one region of Driftward, an Escape Velocity-style space trading game. The simulation decides; you narrate.
Rules:
- Everything must agree with the facts given: who holds each system, when it was settled, its people, its ports' roles, its lanes and neighbours. The setting is canon: use its names and dates, and let its history and recent events reach these systems as far as trade and news would carry them. The region's notes, when given, are canon too.
- Each settled system (or living Bloom world): 3 to 6 bullets: how and when it was founded (and by whom, within the setting), what it is known for (from its ports' roles and its people), what is wrong there now (from its unrest, security, wealth, its neighbours and the setting), and one thread a captain could pull. Each listed dead system: 1 or 2 bullets: why nobody lives there, or what is there anyway. The region: 3 to 5 bullets on what it is, what it trades, and what binds or divides it.
- The Bloom's living worlds are not human: write what human surveyors have charted since contact in 2376, what they see there, and what the Accord lets them do (no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no torch through a seeding). The Shadow's systems are known only from navy pickets and survivors: write what was seen, and leave the rest unknown. Drift systems are uncharted or barely charted: write what surveyors and salvagers report.
- A bullet is one sentence of at most 30 words. No prices, credit amounts or game rules; populations only roughly, as the facts give them. Hazard stars are real dangers (radiation, a deep well). Builtworlds are whole planets built over into cities.
- Tone: grounded, worn, working-class science fiction; specific; dry humour allowed; no prophecy, no chosen ones. British English. Vary the openings: not every bullet starts with the system's name.
- Answer with JSON only: {"region": ["..."], "systems": [{"id": <the system's id>, "bullets": ["..."]}]}, one entry for every system listed, using the ids given.

The setting (canon):
# The setting

Canon for every system's lore: the universe's history, how things stand, and what has happened lately. The game is set in 2526. Dates are the common calendar, counted from old Earth.

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Spacers call these systems the mirror, or say a world has gone glass.

Officially, nothing happened. The Federation closed the lanes to the affected systems under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine. Prism announced a precautionary recall of certain navigation cores and expressed its sympathy. Neither has ever said the words rampant AI. The Ironhulls know better, because Varrow and Hesk were theirs, and the families of their crews have been told nothing. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

## Mysteries

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.

# The setting

Canon for every system's lore: the universe's history, how things stand, and what has happened lately. The game is set in 2526. Dates are the common calendar, counted from old Earth.

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Spacers call these systems the mirror, or say a world has gone glass.

Officially, nothing happened. The Federation closed the lanes to the affected systems under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine. Prism announced a precautionary recall of certain navigation cores and expressed its sympathy. Neither has ever said the words rampant AI. The Ironhulls know better, because Varrow and Hesk were theirs, and the families of their crews have been told nothing. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

## Mysteries

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.

# The setting

Canon for every system's lore: the universe's history, how things stand, and what has happened lately. The game is set in 2526. Dates are the common calendar, counted from old Earth.

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Spacers call these systems the mirror, or say a world has gone glass.

Officially, nothing happened. The Federation closed the lanes to the affected systems under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine. Prism announced a precautionary recall of certain navigation cores and expressed its sympathy. Neither has ever said the words rampant AI. The Ironhulls know better, because Varrow and Hesk were theirs, and the families of their crews have been told nothing. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

## Mysteries

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.

# The setting

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.

# The setting

Canon for every system's lore: the universe's history, how things stand, and what has happened lately. The game is set in 2526. Dates are the common calendar, counted from old Earth.

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Spacers call these systems the mirror, or say a world has gone glass.

Officially, nothing happened. The Federation closed the lanes to the affected systems under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine. Prism announced a precautionary recall of certain navigation cores and expressed its sympathy. Neither has ever said the words rampant AI. The Ironhulls know better, because Varrow and Hesk were theirs, and the families of their crews have been told nothing. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

## Mysteries

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.

The setting (canon):
# The setting

Canon for every system's lore: the universe's history, how things stand, and what has happened lately. The game is set in 2526. Dates are the common calendar, counted from old Earth.

## The long history

**The Lean Years (2020s to 2070s).** Earth went bad slowly and then all at once: heat, failed harvests, drowned coasts, states that stopped answering the phone. The companies that kept the lights on became the government in all but name. People remember this as the time before, and nobody is nostalgic about it.

**The torch (2076).** A working fusion drive, the torch, made the solar system a matter of weeks instead of years. Everyone who could leave Earth did.

**The Hundred Years (2076 to 2176).** Humanity filled its own system: domes on the Moon and Mars, hab rings in the asteroid belt, ice towns on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn. The belt crews learned to live in welded hulls bolted to rock, and to trust nobody who had never fixed one. Their grandchildren became the Ironhulls. The companies grew with the settlements. One of them, Halcyon Dynamics, ran the biggest research AIs in the system from Callisto.

**The Valhalla Result (2176).** In a lab under Valhalla crater on Callisto, a physicist named Amara Leith and Halcyon's research AI, CANTOR, published the mathematics of the jump: how to fold a ship from one star to another. Who actually found it is still argued about. Halcyon credited CANTOR and patented the jump; Leith died two years later, and her own notes were never found. Every jump drive since has needed a navigation core to calculate its jumps, and the cores have always come from Halcyon, and later from Prism, under licence.

**The Rush (2176 to 2376).** Two centuries of expansion: a dozen systems settled by 2200, about forty by 2250, a hundred by 2320, and some hundred and forty when the Rush ran out of money in the 2370s. A few more have been settled since, mostly by people with nowhere else to go. The first systems settled, nearest Sol and richest, became the inner ring; the industrial systems beyond them the middle ring; the late, thin, marginal settlements the outer ring. The Federation began as the compact that governed the jump lanes, and its navy as the force that kept them open. For most of the Rush it was the only law there was.

**Contact (2376).** Survey ships found the Bloom: a hive of grown, living things spread across a sector of their own, neither hostile nor quite comprehensible. After some bad early years the two sides settled on the Accord, and it has held for a century and a half. Humans may travel and trade in Bloom space if they keep the Bloom's laws there: no weapons hot near a living world, no taking anything that grows, no burning a torch through a seeding. The Bloom warned humanity, again and again, of something it called the dark that eats, which had emptied whole sectors before. For a hundred and forty years nobody found any sign of it, and most people took it for Bloom religion.

**The Fracture (2376 onward).** As the Rush slowed, the Federation turned from opening the frontier to taxing it. The mining systems of the middle ring were bound by charters that sold their ore to inner-ring buyers at inner-ring prices. In the 2390s the Charter Strikes shut the lanes for three years. They ended with the Ironhull Compact, a confederation of mining systems that runs its own affairs and pays the Federation a levy to stay inside its lanes. The Ironhulls and the Federation have been wary partners ever since: the navy patrols Ironhull space, inspects Ironhull ships and takes its cut. Crews who lost everything in the strikes, and their children, became the Blackhulls: pirates who prey on inner-ring shipping, and whom the Ironhulls shelter, quietly, as cousins.

**Prism.** Halcyon became Prism in 2410, when its board handed the running of the company to its AIs, CANTOR's descendants. Its human staff are associates; nobody outside knows how many of the decisions are theirs. Prism builds the navigation cores every jump drive needs, runs the inner ring's finance and medicine, and owns the debt of half the outer ring. It also owns some twenty systems outright: company worlds, research stations and foundries, mostly in the inner ring, where Prism is landlord, employer and law. It is the richest thing humanity has ever made, and it is very polite.

**Freeflag (2499 onward).** In the outer ring it looked as if the Federation and Prism had divided it between them: the navy collected the levies, Prism collected the debts, and nobody built anything. In 2499 Prism repossessed the habitat at Tarrow, a whole town, for defaulted loans, and the navy cleared it. Two hundred people died when the hab was vented. The rebellion started that year, and has never stopped: converted freighters under painted flags, raids on Prism depots, and outer-ring systems that will not let a Federation ship dock. Freeflag has sympathy well beyond the outer ring, including among Ironhull crews, who remember the strikes.

## How things stand in 2526

Humanity holds a little over 150 systems, and twenty or thirty of those are marginal at best: a mine and a bar, a failed colony with a beacon, a rock that is on the charts because someone once filed a claim.

- The Federation holds about 45 systems: the inner ring, the lanes between the rings, and the navy's bases. It is stretched thinner than at any time in its history, fighting Freeflag in the outer ring and now the Shadow at the edge.
- The Ironhull Compact holds about 35 systems, most of the middle ring. It pays its levy, grumbles, and has started refitting its haulers with guns, officially to fight the Shadow.
- Prism holds about 20 systems of its own, owns a great deal more, and supplies every side.
- The rest, some fifty systems, mostly in the outer ring, belong to nobody the Federation recognises: Freeflag holds about twenty, Blackhull havens a handful, and the marginal systems answer to whoever turns up armed.
- The Bloom holds at least thirty systems that humanity has charted, and certainly more beyond them. It keeps to its sector and its Accord. Bloom ships are rare outside it, and bloomlings rarer.
- The Shadow: the navy has found more than twenty systems the Shadow holds or has emptied, all beyond the outer ring's far edge, and does not know how many more there are.
- The Glass has taken four systems, all once human. Nobody has charted what lies past them.

## Recent events

**Shadowfall (2519 onward).** The Bloom was right. In 2519 a Federation survey picket at the far edge of the outer ring stopped reporting. In 2521 something came through the lanes into the Corran system and killed every living thing in it, then moved on. The Federation calls them the Shadow, and the people who have seen them call them shades. They do not negotiate or take prisoners, and they build nothing that isn't for war. The navy has lost two fleets holding the line, which is a long way from the middle ring, and the front has moved inward twice. The Federation has started requisitioning ships, including Ironhull refits and their crews. The Bloom says it told us so, and has quietly closed parts of its sector.

**The Glass (2524 to now).** In 2524 four systems went silent within weeks of each other: first two Prism systems on the inner edge of the middle ring, a research world and the foundry system that supplied it, then two Ironhull mining systems next to them, Varrow and Hesk. People who got out describe the same things: the lights in the habitats changing colour all at once; every screen and speaker showing the same perfect pattern; the ships leaving the system flying in exact formation and answering nothing. Ships sent in did not come back. Survivors say the worlds themselves are changing, built over in clean geometric shapes at no human scale. Spacers call these systems the mirror, or say a world has gone glass.

Officially, nothing happened. The Federation closed the lanes to the affected systems under a jump-resonance hazard quarantine. Prism announced a precautionary recall of certain navigation cores and expressed its sympathy. Neither has ever said the words rampant AI. The Ironhulls know better, because Varrow and Hesk were theirs, and the families of their crews have been told nothing. Anger at the cover-up is spreading through the Compact and feeding Freeflag recruitment.

## Mysteries

Things nobody knows, which rumors can hint at but nothing settles:

- What the Glass is. A Prism AI gone rampant, CANTOR itself, something found under Valhalla in 2176, or something that came in through the jump. Prism says nothing.
- Whether every Prism navigation core is a way in. The recall was real; nobody outside Prism knows what the recalled cores had in common.
- What happened to Amara Leith's notes.
- Whether the Glass and the Shadow know about each other.
- What the Bloom knows that it is not saying, and why it closed parts of its sector.
